prize_parts.citation: for introducing firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory, and so changing our understanding of the gains from trade

statement.case_for: I keep B048 first after reading the openings. It meets the test I find most useful across fields: did the work change what we know and how we know it? The heterogeneous-firm framework changed the unit of analysis in trade from the industry to the firm. It identified a new channel for gains from trade, namely reallocation toward more productive firms. It also made firm-level micro data a standard empirical tool, which ties theory to evidence in an unusually direct way. The core predictions have been tested in many countries and datasets over more than twenty years, so the maturity question is largely settled. Melitz (2003) is the identifiable core. Helpman's work with Melitz and Yeaple on exporting versus FDI, and his broader earlier trade theory, make the two-name credit coherent and separable. I prefer to keep the credit tight rather than add a third name with a distinct and later contribution.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum developed closely parallel firm-level trade ideas and evidence, and none of them is on this ballot entry. A Melitz-Helpman credit could therefore be read as favouring the theory over the empirical foundations. Some welfare conclusions also depend on functional-form assumptions, such as Pareto productivity. Trade also received a prize in 2008, though for different work. Finally, I am relying on my own knowledge of the literature and have not independently verified any source.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B048 third and would credit Redding as a third laureate, alongside Melitz and Helpman, for quantitative and spatial extensions of the framework.
responses.response: I take the point that Redding's work is important and has had a large effect on how trade and economic geography are modelled. I would still keep it out of this citation. His contribution is a later wave built on the heterogeneous-firm framework, and the quantitative and spatial strand is a separate discovery. Adding a third name would blur the citation, and it would make the later strand look like part of the original achievement. My own research on regional economic geography makes me wary of overweighting that strand by familiarity. If the committee wants to recognise the quantitative-spatial agenda, it should treat it as a distinct achievement later on.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B048 second. She flags that the parallel Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum line is not on this ballot, and that trade was recognised in 2008, so the committee might prefer other fields.
responses.response: I agree that the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum priority question is the main attribution risk, and I list it among my uncertainties. I do not think it changes the structure of the credit. Melitz (2003) supplies the general-equilibrium model of selection and reallocation, and Helpman supplies the extensions to exporting versus FDI. I would not let the 2008 prize count against merit here, because it recognised the earlier new trade theory with increasing returns and love of variety, which is a different discovery. Field balance can inform timing, but it is not evidence about this work.

responses.point: Strömberg ranks B001 first. He says law and finance combined cross-country data with a clear theoretical framing and reshaped corporate finance, comparative law and development. He also acknowledges the measurement criticisms.
responses.response: I agree that the reach is exceptional, and I rank B001 fifth, so I do not dismiss it. The difference is how the central claim has survived scrutiny. The legal-origins hypothesis is contested on causal identification, on how legal rules were coded, and on whether legal origin proxies for deeper historical factors. As an economic historian, I find that last point a serious concern. The heterogeneous-firm framework has had its functional forms criticised, but its core qualitative predictions have held up in many datasets. I would also want the committee to settle the Vishny question before settling the merits of B001. I keep it as an alternative, not as my preferred part.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B049 first. He regards Persson, Tabellini and Besley as founding modern political economics, with mature, replicated work, and he asks whether the 2024 institutions prize creates overlap.
responses.response: I rank B049 second and agree on the foundational standing of the programme. I share the concern about thematic overlap with the 2024 prize, and that is why B048 stays ahead of it for me. The identification of cross-country constitutional and electoral-rule effects is also more contested than the evidence behind firm selection. I would want to know whether the committee sees the constitutions work and Besley's state-capacity work as one achievement or two. Because the configuration allows at most three people in total, the two achievements cannot both be rewarded in this simulation, so I name B049 as an alternative and not as a second part.

uncertainties: Whether the committee should extend the credit to Bernard, Eaton, Jensen or Kortum, who are not on this ballot entry.
Whether Redding's quantitative and spatial work should be credited with this achievement or treated as a later and separate one.
How much the welfare conclusions depend on functional-form assumptions such as Pareto productivity.
Whether the legal-origins critique is decisive for B001, and whether Vishny's omission is acceptable at a three-name cap.
Whether thematic overlap with the 2024 institutions prize should weigh against B049.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. No documented personal tie to Melitz or Helpman appears. My field is economic history and regional growth, which is adjacent to Redding's spatial work. That is a matter of research proximity, not a personal connection, and I have kept him out of my preferred credit. Committee colleague Tommy Andersson is at Lund and ranks B049 first, which I note for transparency. I have worked with political scientist Johannes Lindvall, but no candidate is connected to him. I do not claim independent verification of any source.
